facts.text: 事業者が紹介プログラムを自動で運営するためのソフト。紹介リンク、紹介の追跡、報酬の条件と払い出しの管理をまとめる。全プランに、紹介制度の設定を支援する専任アドバイザーが付く。住宅・専門サービス、医療、金融、フランチャイズ、複数店舗、SaaS、ECなどが使う。
創業者Josh Hoは2013年に、小さな事業が自前で紹介プログラムを運営できる道具を思いつき、同年12月にドメインを登録した。ベータ期は家族を支えるため、ソフトの受託を副業で続けた。旧製品UberNoteの利用者リスト、Betalist、知人で告知し、2014年前半には200超の接点、最初の1年半で500社超が登録した。作業は月約20時間。
最初の管理画面はSurvey Monkeyの回答フォームで、最初の版は古いHTMLの雛形と使い回しのコードで作った。本人は、出せずに終わった企画が少なくとも5つあるとも書く。客の話を聞いて気に入らない内容が出ても、作りたい製品の像を優先してまず出した。
2015年6月に月59ドルの有料版を公開し、2日以内に最初の有料客が登録、月末には4社になった。数か月で月約2,000ドルのMRRに達し、創業者は専業になった。
2016年2月、ギフトカード報酬の処理を足し、月250ドル・6か月契約の上位プランを設けた。1社から一度に1,500ドルが入った。任意の「サクセス支援パッケージ」も作り、後に月払いでは必須にした。
2016年7月に最初の営業を雇ったが、研修と顧客理解の不足で失敗し、2か月分の売上を失った。10月に2人目の営業を雇い、2016年末は顧客170社、常勤換算で3.5人分の体制、MRR約15,000ドル。外部資金は受けていない。
2019年5月の本人の投稿は、月の売上が70,000ドルに達したと書き、要因は2人目の営業の採用だったとする。リードが足りるか心配で数か月迷ったが、採用後はサイトの文面・LP・申込ボタンを直してリードを増やした。
2019年7月の投稿は、導入時の立ち上げ会議と客ごとの専任サクセス担当で解約を半分に減らしたと書く。客には「代わりにやる」でなく「手伝う」と明確に伝えている。8月の投稿は、4か月連続でMRRが5%ずつ伸びたと書く。
現在のOperatorプランは月250ドル。長期契約は不要、年払いは10%引き、専任アドバイザーとその支援チームが込みで、初期設定料は無い。
2025年10月23日の更新で、紹介先訪問・会員訪問・紹介担当者データの書き出しを追加した（上限は標準50,000行）。

Under the Rock
From beta to real business – Discovering inside sales
(2015-2017) Referral Rock's story from beta -> real business in 3 years with no funding, an all remote team, and never leaving my chair (kinda)
10 min read
February 21, 2019
By
Josh Ho
ON THIS PAGE
Growing from an idea to business takes time, a lot of time! Especially when you are stubborn, don’t want to take funding, are more risk-averse than people think, and initially think you can do everything yourself. If you ever get that lucky, there is a lot you go through learning about yourself and other people (team and customers) to have the idea take flight to a fully sustainable business.
Back in 2013, the idea of providing small businesses with the tools to run their own referral program was born. Not too long after in December 2013, referralrock.com was registered.
Beta, MVP, and Launch (2014)
So many lessons learned from my past in building a startup led to Referral Rock. Like most businesses, the first few months of Referral Rock were focused on building the initial contacts and defining an ideal target market. All during this beta period, I was software consulting on the side to support myself and my family.
MVP
I want to say I formally went through a customer development process, but that’s not entirely true. The truth is I didn’t like what I heard from the initial group, and I had a vision for what I wanted the product to be, so I built an MVP anyway. As many projects die on the vine (at least five that never launched), I was at least smart enough to not put too much into the MVP. The first version I cobbled together was from some old HTML templates and some reusable code laying around; then I was off.
Survey Monkey was my first admin UI, where I used it as a form to complete a user’s program (i.e., logo, tagline, business name, referral offer). I then exported it to a CSV, then converted it to a resource file to match a subdomain in the system. If they wanted changes, I manually made them upon request. It was quick and dirty but saved me a lot of time to get something out to people without too much coding investment.
Lack of a launch
Sites like Product Hunt weren’t as big of a thing in 2014, and this was a time where listing sites still had a little weight. Sites like Betalist , personal contacts, and even the list of users from UberNote were used to get the word out. I didn’t care much about a big launch at this point as I was excited about the project but wasn’t confident it could be a business yet.
Within the first half of 2014, Referral Rock had a list of over 200 contacts. Referral Rock’s beta program had begun, and we had some live fire and opened the site up for registration. During this time, Referral Rock was a part-time gig, and working hours consisted of working nights and weekends. Thinking back, I’d estimate I was working about 20 hours a month on the project.
With over 500 businesses signed up, the first year and a half proved to me that there were customers in this market and that there was a need for the software.
Paying customers (June 2015)
I was chatting with a longtime startup friend of mine (Alex Black) with great excitement about everything I had done with Referral Rock, and he burst my bubble by mentioning this wasn’t a business unless I charged people. Initially, I was upset, but then I took that candid advice and turned it into a challenge to create a paid version overnight .
In June of 2015, the first paid version was launched. As luck would have it, the first paying customer signed up within two days! Beta users still had access, but sign-ups were now only for the paid version ($59 per month). By the end of the first month, I had four paying customers, and I was on cloud nine!
Thinking back, it makes me wonder how fragile I was at that point. If the paid version was up and there were no takers for a month or so, I’m not sure if my impatience would have gotten the best of me or not.
Over the next few months, I slowly shut down the beta program. I made it clear up front that we would eventually charge, but I highly valued my early users. As I closed out the program, I emailed the most active beta users and sent them a coupon with a massive discount for life. I firmly believe in grandfathering all pricing as a sign of the gratitude and appreciation for anyone that has taken an early bet on us; it’s something we’ve continued to this day.
I was on my way to the dream of building a little internet business that I could provide recurring income for my family and me. Within a few months, Referral Rock was making about $2k a month, and I reached a tipping point for myself. All I wanted to do was work on Referral Rock, and doing any other consulting work was starting to feel like a drag or even torture as I rushed through projects. I decided to make the jump to full-time.
Discovered “Inside Sales”
Can I build a product and sell it to thousands of people and never have to actually talk to them? That’s the indie hacker dream, right? Well… when all your income is coming in small bite-sized chunks, and your marketing efforts are starting to normalize, you begin to follow the path presented. If I weren’t forced to need the money, maybe I would have continued down the road of a more self-service-oriented product.
I started out doing all product support through chat, but then frustration set in, and I had those moments where I realized I was either going to spend the next 20 minutes on chat trying to explain something, or I could pick up the phone/screen share and talk to them to have the problem solved in 5 minutes. Path of least resistance? I picked up the phone.
Within a week, I found that talking to people in person resulted in more sales. In fact, the conversion rate practically tripled. I put up a demo request form and found that I needed to leave half my time open to scheduling demos. Who would have thought that actually talking to people and explaining the product and service in person is the key?! Brilliant, right?
It wasn’t until much later that I realized this was inside sales and founder selling at its finest. It was the birth of our consultative sales practices and laid the groundwork for what would genuinely get Referral Rock off the ground.
Getting bigger than just me
After inside sales were implemented and made an integral part of the sales process, it was evident that we needed to grow the team. At this point, I felt confident that customers could be acquired, we could provide value, and there was enough revenue coming in to support a business. More hands were needed as I would no longer be able to go at it alone.
The jump to building a team was scary as it wasn’t just me in the boat anymore. Yes, I had a family but was always confident I could provide, but bringing other people with me and having them depend on me was a different sort of risk. In the early days, I brought on some part-time people and others willing to take a chance on nights and weekends. As we grew in revenue, so did my confidence in bringing people on full-time.
In this time frame, there were moments where I kept wondering and having doubts. How big is this market? Last month we had 20 new customers, and this month there are only 10… Is this the new normal? This is around the time I discovered SaaStr, specifically through this post about 10 unaffiliated customers , and I no longer felt alone in what I was doing.
I now find it interesting to compare how my startup beliefs changed on what was truly important for the business. Referral Rock did more in revenue in 1.5 years with a single founder than UberNote did in 4 years with a team of 4, some funding, and an accelerator. Not quite an apples-to-apples comparison, but a very different change in focus on revenue and sustainability vs. user acquisition and market share.
By the end of 2015, Referral Rock hired its first team member and got some outside technical assistance from an old high school friend as the business grew to 50 customers. So that put us at 2 FTEs across 3 people at $3k MRR.
Muscle development with customers and sales (January 2016)
Though the business had grown quite a bit, 2016 proved to be the real year of change for me. I wasn’t just coding anymore. As an engineer by trade, I was developing more skills in sales, marketing, and managing customers. This wasn’t totally foreign to me as I previously had a software consulting business, but that was dealing with 2-3 customers in a given month vs. having conversations and managing over 100 in a month. I had to grow all kinds of different muscles and fast.
Listening to customers
Listening to customers isn’t just about what features to build and listening to their feedback. It’s also about getting a feel for them and understanding their needs, even if they are not saying it.
During this period, I was splitting my time between inside sales and developing the product. I had some early team members helping out, writing KB articles and marketing blog posts to support me.
In February 2016, Referral Rock raised the prices for the first time. I remember the day this all happened. I was on a call with a prospect hearing about how their sales process worked and how they were already using referrals. They spoke of the pain of issuing rewards and how much time it took to manage the referrals and rewards.
Reward fulfillment was a feature that we were considering, but we weren’t sure our $59 a month customer would really care. After they mentioned referral rewards in the amount of hundreds of dollars, I realized how much a new customer was worth to them and how trusting a $59 a month startup seemed iffy at best.
By the time we had our next call, I had added gift cards fulfillment to a new higher-priced plan at $250 a month with a 6-month commitment on our pricing page. I wasn’t quite sure how the next call would go as I was sure the price jump would scare the customer away. To my surprise, she mentioned she saw the new plan on the website and was happy to sign up. At that point, we were making $3.5k per month and just took in $1.5k in one swoop. This was a massive change vs. the microtransactions I was previously receiving. Maybe I can afford to pay a salesperson instead of me?
Scale-out sales (Attempt #1)
June quickly approached. Referral Rock hit a significant milestone as the anniversary of the ‘pay’ version arrived. During this time, the business grew to a total of 110 customers. It was then when I realized that so much time was taken up by sales demos and the product was developing much slower.
We needed to scale out sales! July came, and the first salesperson was hired. At this point, all I knew was what I was doing in sales but never considered myself an actual salesperson. I thought a salesperson was supposed to be “salesy” and what I was doing was a hack. So the first person I hired fit that mold, and as you probably can guess… I failed miserably for these key reasons:
We had ZERO onboarding and training for sales – I didn’t realize how much of a learning curve a new product and new customer profile mattered. I thought hiring a salesperson was just going to spin up and do what they do as a “real salesperson” in a matter of weeks. I think I even gave the new salesperson all the demos within about 2 weeks.
We didn’t have the right type of salesperson – There are different types of salespeople? My first hire had experience selling to SMBs, which was great, but didn’t have much marketing experience, which led to some challenges in picking up on the product and understanding the customer.
This was a hard lesson to learn as it killed 2 months of revenue, and I was pulled back into sales and lost valuable time and energy that could have gone to other areas of the business.
Scale-out sales (Attempt #2)
In October of 2016, it was time to take another at-bat. This time the training process, though still not 100% settled, was in a much better spot. In hindsight, we were actually very lucky in more than one way with finding our next salesperson.
First, he actually found us. Mica was in limbo with his own startup. He didn’t want to give up on it, but couldn’t work on it full time either. So, he stumbled upon a Referral Rock listing and decided to reach out. He said right away that he could help with everything we needed and threw down the gauntlet by saying he could do anything I could do except code. I told him he didn’t know what he was getting into, but go ahead and put your money where your mouth is.
Second, Mica turned out to be much more than our first salesperson outside of me. He was just what we needed to get to the next level as he eventually took up the helm running both sales and what would become customer success.
By December, we were able to begin focusing on other areas of the business. Since sales had a new head honcho, it allowed the rest of the team members to dig into their core duties.
Pushing on customer pricing
With the help of Mica holding down the day-to-day sales and customer success, we were able to land our first large enterprise sale. It was for a lot of custom work on our end that honestly wasn’t even on the roadmap. So I priced it high because I viewed it as a distraction, but for the right amount, it could be worth it. This was a mental pricing exercise I learned from my consulting days that we still use today. Price it, so you’re happy if you win, but not upset if you lose. In this case, I priced it high enough that it was worth the distraction, and when the customer accepted, I was happy with it. In retrospect, it was a big distraction but added enough cash to the balance sheet for me to feel more comfortable pushing forward with some new hires.
Another significant change to the pricing model was that we added a new “Customer Success Package.” We started charging for most as a way to justify all the time we took to help customers use the product correctly and launch their programs. First, it was optional, then quickly moved it to a required setup fee for month-to-month commitments. Conversions to paid did not drop, and churn was reduced. Win-win! As a bonus, we also waived the fee for a longer commitment and got many converts to 6+ month contracts (yay cashflow).
The year ended with a total of 170 customers, 3.5 FTE, and $15k MRR. By this time, I stopped asking myself if this was sustainable and if this was a real business. The answer was a resounding yes! It only took 1.5 years of sales and 1,000 demos and trial users for me to believe.
Key lessons so far:
Let the customers and business unfold as you go
By listening to the customers and their needs, it’s led Referral Rock to be a totally different business from what I intended. The business has a life of its own and won’t necessarily end up where you designed, and that can be a good thing! We have gone from being a $50 per month self-service product meant to require little to no interaction, to being intimately involved in building relationships with our customers and their success and building a team.
Everything takes longer than you think
“In a month we can train a sales team with no materials, a founder shooting from the hip, and still keep up with existing sales”… Dying words! Don’t take for granted how long it takes to get people up to speed on everything that you’ve learned over 2 years.
Everything slows down as you have customers. You have a drag of legacy customers, legacy features, that have to be managed as you grow. Your existing customers are what keep you alive, and they are the ones who invested in you early. Don’t piss them off!

Cut our churn in 1/2
Personalized on-boarding and dedicated customer success per account have helped us cut our churn in 1/2. We took the time and build a process around helping customers reach their goals.
We've always had a consultative inside sale, but in the early days just let them loose on the product after the sale and was reactive with support. Our on-boarding process is now a pro-active approach where we have a kick-off meeting and complete a profile on the customer.
You have to make it very clear to the customers and set the proper expectations. For example, we make it extremely clear to the customers throughout the whole process that "we help you" not "do for you".
Every SaaS business wants low/no touch these days, but customers do want personalized help. It may not work for every SaaS business as its very dependent on their pricing and type of customers they are attracting, but it's something you may want to do in the early days.
As an added benefit, our CSMs are exceptional contributors with product and customer feedback for both qualitative and quantitative information so we can build-in high impact features and functionality.

Mistakes with my first sales hire
We needed to scale out sales! July came and the first salesperson was hired. At this point, all I knew was what I was doing in sales but never considered myself an actual salesperson. I thought a salesperson was supposed to be “salesy” and what I was doing was a hack. So the first person I hired fit that mold and as you probably can guess… I failed miserably...
Overall these were some mistakes with my first sales hire that hopefully others don't have to repeat.
We had ZERO onboarding and training for sales.
I didn’t realize how much of a learning curve a new product and new customer profile mattered. I thought hiring a salesperson was just going to spin up and do what they do as a “real salesperson” in a matter of weeks. I think I even gave the new salesperson all the demos within about 2 weeks. Here's what I learned...
Build out at least the framework of some training, record more of my own demos, and come up with a basic level script that someone could pick up rather quickly.
We didn’t have the right type of salesperson
There are different types of salespeople? My first hire had experience selling to SMBs which was great but didn’t have much marketing experience which led to some challenges on picking up on the product and understanding the customer. Here's what I learned...
Get rid of the picture in your head of what a sales person looks like, it will cloud your hiring judgement. Find someone who is coachable, understands at least the basics of digital marketing, is consultative and helpful vs salesy and pushy.
This was a hard lesson to learn as it killed 2 months of revenue and I was pulled back into sales and lost valuable time and energy that could have gone to other areas of the business.
(Also note this was all 2.5 years ago. I added this milestone retroactively when filling out the product profile. I didn't know it would all show up here like it was current)

Weighing it yourself? Here's an honest breakdown of building a referral program yourself vs. using Referral Rock .
Referral program software FAQs
What is Referral Rock?
Referral Rock is a software service that businesses use to run their referral programs. Signing up or logging in from here is not joining a referral program. This site is for businesses who want to run one.
What is referral program software?
Referral program software provides what a business needs to run an automated referral program: a member portal, reward rules, payout management, and much more, all to help you get more referrals.
Is Referral Rock a refer-a-friend platform?
Yes. Refer-a-friend is the customer referral program type, and Referral Rock runs it end to end: customers are enrolled automatically, every referral is tracked back to the person who sent it, and both sides can be rewarded. The same platform also runs brand ambassador and partner or affiliate programs, so one tool covers all three.
Is a referral program right for my business?
The best sign you're ready is that customers already refer you on their own, even informally. A referral program organizes and rewards that word of mouth, so it works best when there's already some enthusiasm to build on and you have room to take on more business.
How you sell matters more than what industry you're in. See the readiness check for the honest version of who a program fits, and who it doesn't.
Should I build a referral program myself or use software?
You can start with a spreadsheet and manual payouts, and many businesses do. A spreadsheet usually holds up until the program grows, then tracking who referred whom, preventing fraud, and paying rewards on time becomes real, ongoing work.
Software takes over the parts that don't scale. We wrote an honest breakdown of the tradeoffs in building a referral program yourself vs. using Referral Rock .
How long does it take to see referrals coming in?
First referrals usually arrive within the first few weeks of launch. How fast depends on the size of your existing customer base and how you promote the program. Your advisor helps you work that out before you go live.
How can I create a referral website?
Our software makes it simple to create a referral website. We provide customizable landing and sharing pages so you can quickly set up a dedicated site for your program.
You can add sign-up forms, referral tracking, and reward information, and many of our clients launch a working referral website in just a few hours.
How does referral tracking integrate with my existing systems?
Our referral tracking software connects to popular CRMs, e-commerce, and marketing platforms through pre-built integrations. Data flows both ways between your referral program and your other systems, so tracking stays accurate without manual work.
Is it difficult to set up and manage a client referral program?
Modern referral program software is built to be user-friendly. Our platform offers templates and guided setup, so businesses of all sizes can launch and manage effective programs without deep technical knowledge.
Many of our clients are up and running within hours, on their own or with help from a dedicated advisor.
What are best practices for implementing referral software?
Start with the fundamentals that separate programs that grow from programs that stall. Reward both sides, not just the referrer. In our analysis of 952 programs, 54% rewarded only the referrer, leaving the friend with no reason to act.
Send people to a personalized referral page instead of your homepage, and invite customers while they're still excited. One Referral Rock customer saw 86% of their referrals come within the first 90 days.
Promote continuously rather than relying on a single launch email, and lean on the dedicated advisor included with every plan to put these in place before you go live.
What are the most common referral program mistakes to avoid?
Across 952 programs we've analyzed over 9 years, the biggest killers are inconsistent promotion after launch (behind 82% of stalled programs), rewarding only the referrer, and sending referred friends to a generic homepage or checkout form with no context (which 42% of programs do).
Fixing those three is usually what keeps a program producing referrals month after month instead of stalling out.
How can I promote my referral program to maximize participation?
Treat referral as an ongoing system, not a one-time campaign. We recommend the 3 P's of continuous promotion: Proactive Invites (reach out right after a customer milestone), Passive Entry Points (make the program easy to find across your site, emails, and checkout), and Program Recruiters (let frontline and service teams enroll customers directly).
Referral Rock automates ongoing campaigns that target only the customers who haven't joined yet, so promotion keeps running without manual effort.
What rewards and incentives work best for referrals?
Reward choice depends on your audience, but the data points in clear directions. Two-sided rewards, something for both the referrer and the friend, consistently outperform one-sided ones, yet most programs still reward only the referrer.
Among Referral Rock customers, gift cards are the most popular member reward (61%), while referred friends respond best to discounts and gift cards. Most programs use fixed amounts (92%) rather than a percentage of the sale, which keeps budgeting simple.
How can I measure the ROI of my online referral program?
Our referral program tracking captures the metrics that matter: shares, unique people reached, referrals generated, conversion rates, customer acquisition cost through referrals, lifetime value of referred customers, and overall program revenue and costs.
What results can I expect from a referral program?
Results vary by business, but referral traffic is high-intent. Among Referral Rock programs, referred visitors who become customers typically do so within about a day, each share reaches roughly 13 people, and programs average around 1,388 monthly website sessions from referral sources.
Manage the leading indicators (shares, then reach, then referrals) rather than waiting on the final count. Our analytics dashboard, brand-visit tracking, and data exports give you the numbers to prove ROI.
How secure is a referral system?
Security is a top priority. Our referral system includes data encryption, secure reward distribution, and full compliance with relevant data-protection regulations like GDPR and CCPA, and we update our protocols regularly to keep your data and your customers' information protected.
Does Referral Rock help prevent fraudulent referrals?
Yes. Referral Rock includes fraud detection and prevention: IP tracking, duplicate-entry detection, and suspicious-activity monitoring to protect the integrity of your program. Clients see meaningful reductions in fraudulent activity after switching to our system.
How much does referral software typically cost?
Referral Rock is one simple plan: the Operator Plan at $250 a month, with unlimited referrals and a dedicated referral expert included. There's no free plan, but you can try everything on a free trial before you commit. Add-ons cover the features not everyone needs, so you only pay for what you need.
Enterprise and Multi-Org plans cover large brands and multi-location or franchise networks.

FAQs
What is a member? A member is one unique email address in your program.
What is a referral? A referral is when a member shares your program and someone takes action, such as signing up, making a purchase, or completing a form.
What are base members? Base members are the members you add yourself: manual imports, CSV uploads, and one-off additions. The Operator Plan includes 10,000, and you can buy more. Rolling members from automated sources never draw from base members.
What are rolling members? Rolling members are members that get added from automated sources: web forms, HubSpot, Salesforce, Zapier, or the API. You get 1,000 free each month. The allowance resets monthly and doesn't carry over. Rolling members don't count against base members.
Do disabled members count against my limits? No. When an email address stops working, that member is disabled automatically. Disabled members do not count against any limit.
Are referrals really unlimited? Yes. There are no referral caps or overage fees on the Operator Plan. The price stays $250 a month at any referral volume.
Do I need my own email tool or website? No. Referral Rock sends the invites, reminders, and reward emails, and hosts the member portal and landing pages. You can connect the tools you already run, but nothing else is required.
What does the program advisor help with? Your advisor designs the program with you: the reward structure, the messaging your members see, and the integration setup. After launch, the same advisor keeps reviewing performance with you.
Is there an onboarding fee? No. The dedicated program advisor and their team are included with every plan.
Which integrations are included? The Operator Plan includes the integrations that connect with field mapping: email tools, billing systems, and e-commerce platforms. Anything more advanced gets scoped with your advisor.
What rewards can I offer? Coupons, pay-as-you-go gift cards, or custom rewards you fulfill yourself.
Is Referral Rock only for tech companies? No. Referral Rock works for any business that earns customers through word of mouth. Home services, professional services, e-commerce, financial services, healthcare, and real estate all run on the Operator Plan.
What if I have multiple brands, locations, or franchises? Multiple brands, locations, and franchises have their own plans. The Enterprise Plan scales one brand past standard volume. The Multi-Org Plan runs a separate program for each brand, location, or client under one account. The Enterprise & Multi-Org pricing page covers both.
Can I try it before paying? Yes. There's a free 14-day trial. You can explore the software and design a program during it.

Hey it's Mica,
We get a lot of requests from customers asking for more data. Last month, we asked readers about their biggest pain points and over 35% said "Getting Data / Reports on Activity" topped their list. We love data and are always happy to provide it where we can.
That’s why we made it easier to report on more of your data with three new data exports (without waiting on us):
Referral Visits - Track how your program is being shared and how referrals interact with your site
Member Visits - Analyze how members discover and engage with your program
Recruiter Data - See how many members and referrals each recruiter works with
Use these exports to further analyze your programs or drop them into your preferred analytics/AI tool to surface new insights.
Let's dive in. 👇👇
-Mica
Head of Operations
🔗 Referral Visit Export
A referral visit happens when someone clicks a member's share link and visits your site or referral page.
Use this data to:
Identify which share methods (email, social, direct link) convert best
Understand how long a referral spends on your site
Find friction points in your referral journey
Spot high-intent visitors to investigate their full visit history
What's included in the export:
Referral Details - Date, Visitor ID, Referral ID, Email
Member Attribution (who referred them) - Name, Email, Member ID
Engagement Metrics - Page Views, Session Length
Traffic Sources - Source, Medium, Country
Open Referral Visits
🔍 Member Visit Export
A member visit tracks when a member (or potential member) interacts with your referral program, whether logged in or not.
Use this data to:
Find your most engaged members (even if they haven't converted referrals yet)
Spot engagement drop-offs and patterns
Identify which promotion channels drive member activity
See how members interact over time
What's included in the export:
Member Details - Date, Visitor ID, Member ID, Email
Engagement Metrics - # of Views, # of Shares, Visit Type (first-time vs. returning)
Traffic Source - Source, Medium, Country
Open Member Visits
🧑‍🤝‍🧑 Recruiter Data Export
Recruiters are team members (sales reps, customer service, field reps, etc.) who help grow your referral program by signing up new members during 1-on-1 interactions.
Use this data to:
Identify top-performing recruiters and understand what they're doing differently
Spot inactive team members who need coaching or reminders
Build incentive programs based on actual performance
What's included in the export:
Recruiter Details - Recruiter ID, Program, Last Access Date
Member Activity - # of Members Assigned, Last Member Assigned, # of Members Sourced, Last Member Sourced
Referral Activity - # of Referrals Assigned, Last Referral Assigned, # of Referrals Sourced, Last Referral Sourced
Open Reports

sources.title: The Referral Rock Story Part 1: From Beta to Business
Referral Rock（掲載ページと創業者の投稿）

facts.text: 事業者が紹介プログラムを自動で運営するためのソフト。紹介リンク、紹介の追跡、報酬の条件と払い出しの管理をまとめる。全プランに、紹介制度の設定を支援する専任アドバイザーが付く。住宅・専門サービス、医療、金融、フランチャイズ、複数店舗、SaaS、ECなどが使う。
創業者Josh Hoは2013年に、小さな事業が自前で紹介プログラムを運営できる道具を思いつき、同年12月にドメインを登録した。ベータ期は家族を支えるため、ソフトの受託を副業で続けた。旧製品UberNoteの利用者リスト、Betalist、知人で告知し、2014年前半には200超の接点、最初の1年半で500社超が登録した。作業は月約20時間。
最初の管理画面はSurvey Monkeyの回答フォームで、最初の版は古いHTMLの雛形と使い回しのコードで作った。本人は、出せずに終わった企画が少なくとも5つあるとも書く。客の話を聞いて気に入らない内容が出ても、作りたい製品の像を優先してまず出した。
2015年6月に月59ドルの有料版を公開し、2日以内に最初の有料客が登録、月末には4社になった。数か月で月約2,000ドルのMRRに達し、創業者は専業になった。
2016年2月、ギフトカード報酬の処理を足し、月250ドル・6か月契約の上位プランを設けた。1社から一度に1,500ドルが入った。任意の「サクセス支援パッケージ」も作り、後に月払いでは必須にした。
2016年7月に最初の営業を雇ったが、研修と顧客理解の不足で失敗し、2か月分の売上を失った。10月に2人目の営業を雇い、2016年末は顧客170社、常勤換算で3.5人分の体制、MRR約15,000ドル。外部資金は受けていない。
2019年5月の本人の投稿は、月の売上が70,000ドルに達したと書き、要因は2人目の営業の採用だったとする。リードが足りるか心配で数か月迷ったが、採用後はサイトの文面・LP・申込ボタンを直してリードを増やした。
2019年7月の投稿は、導入時の立ち上げ会議と客ごとの専任サクセス担当で解約を半分に減らしたと書く。客には「代わりにやる」でなく「手伝う」と明確に伝えている。8月の投稿は、4か月連続でMRRが5%ずつ伸びたと書く。
現在のOperatorプランは月250ドル。長期契約は不要、年払いは10%引き、専任アドバイザーとその支援チームが込みで、初期設定料は無い。
2025年10月23日の更新で、紹介先訪問・会員訪問・紹介担当者データの書き出しを追加した（上限は標準50,000行）。
